response = "The controversy over the Reichstag fire shows in miniature how historians weigh rival reconstructions of an event whose documentary trail is broken and partisan. The Reichstag building in Berlin was set on fire on the night of 27 February 1933. Because the Nazi government, in the hours that followed, publicly attributed the fire to a communist insurrectionary conspiracy, the result was the Reichstag Fire Decree of 28 February 1933, by which most civil liberties guaranteed by the Weimar constitution were suspended. The decree itself was enacted by a two-thirds majority vote of the Reichstag. Nearly three decades after the fire, in 1962, Fritz Tobias published his book-length study of it. Tobias held a chair in modern history at the University of Göttingen. Tobias argued that van der Lubbe was the sole perpetrator of the arson; that is, his thesis was that no person other than van der Lubbe set the Reichstag alight. Van der Lubbe had accomplices in setting the Reichstag fire, a finding that cannot be squared with the contention that nobody but he put a torch to the building. Adjudication between such accounts is not a matter of preferring the more dramatic story, nor of counting heads among specialists. Historians apply source criticism to test the authenticity, provenance and internal consistency of documents. They treat testimony recorded decades after an event as weaker evidence than contemporaneous records, since recollection decays and late statements are shaped by the very controversies they enter. A sworn 1955 statement by the SA member Hans-Martin Lennings came to light in 2019 in the records of the Hanover public prosecutor's office. Although a deposition set down so long after the night in question carries less evidential weight than a paper drawn up at the time, Lennings's statement asserted that he had driven van der Lubbe to the Reichstag building that night, and that assertion is what demonstrates that the arsonist had the helpers described above. A find of this kind does not merely add a footnote to the prevailing reading; it redistributes the burden of proof, so that the lone-arsonist reconstruction must now be defended rather than assumed, and the consensus that had settled around it is reopened for argument."
